section.paragraph: Many jobs offer an annual cost-of-living increase to keep salaries consistent with inflation. Suppose, for example, a recent college graduate finds a position as a sales manager earning an annual salary of \$26,000. He is promised a 2% cost of living increase each year. His annual salary in any given year can be found by multiplying his salary from the previous year by 102%. His salary will be \$26,520 after one year; \$27,050.40 after two years; \$27,591.41 after three years; and so on. When a salary increases by a constant rate each year, the salary grows by a constant factor. In this section, we will review sequences that grow in this way.
section.heading: Finding Common Ratios
section.paragraph: The yearly salary values described form a geometric sequence because they change by a constant factor each year. Each term of a geometric sequence increases or decreases by a constant factor called the common ratio. The sequence below is an example of a geometric sequence because each term increases by a constant factor of 6. Multiplying any term of the sequence by the common ratio 6 generates the subsequent term.

note.title: Definition of a Geometric Sequence
note.paragraph: A geometric sequence is one in which any term divided by the previous term is a constant. This constant is called the common ratio of the sequence. note.title: Q&A
note.paragraph: If you are told that a sequence is geometric, do you have to divide every term by the previous term to find the common ratio?
No. If you know that the sequence is geometric, you can choose any one term in the sequence and divide it by the previous term to find the common ratio.

section.heading: Writing Terms of Geometric Sequences
section.paragraph: Now that we can identify a geometric sequence, we will learn how to find the terms of a geometric sequence if we are given the first term and the common ratio. The terms of a geometric sequence can be found by beginning with the first term and multiplying by the common ratio repeatedly. For instance, if the first term of a geometric sequence is $$a_{1} = - 2$$ and the common ratio is $$r = 4,$$ we can find subsequent terms by multiplying $$- 2 \cdot 4$$ to get $$- 8$$ then multiplying the result $$- 8 \cdot 4$$ to get $$- 32$$ and so on.

note.title: How To
note.paragraph: Given the first term and the common factor, find the first four terms of a geometric sequence.

list.item: Multiply the initial term, $$a_{1},$$ by the common ratio to find the next term, $$a_{2}.$$
Repeat the process, using $$a_{n} = a_{2}$$ to find $$a_{3}$$ and then $$a_{3}$$ to find $$a_{4,}$$ until all four terms have been identified.
Write the terms separated by commons within brackets.

example.title: Writing the Terms of a Geometric Sequence

problem.paragraph: List the first four terms of the geometric sequence with $$a_{1} = 5$$ and $$r = -2.$$

solution.paragraph: Multiply $$a_{1}$$ by $$- 2$$ to find $$a_{2}.$$ Repeat the process, using $$a_{2}$$ to find $$a_{3},$$ and so on.

section.heading: Using Recursive Formulas for Geometric Sequences
section.paragraph: A recursive formula allows us to find any term of a geometric sequence by using the previous term. Each term is the product of the common ratio and the previous term. For example, suppose the common ratio is 9. Then each term is nine times the previous term. As with any recursive formula, the initial term must be given.

note.title: Q&A
note.paragraph: Do we have to divide the second term by the first term to find the common ratio?

No. We can divide any term in the sequence by the previous term. It is, however, most common to divide the second term by the first term because it is often the easiest method of finding the common ratio.

section.heading: Using Explicit Formulas for Geometric Sequences
section.paragraph: Because a geometric sequence is an exponential function whose domain is the set of positive integers, and the common ratio is the base of the function, we can write explicit formulas that allow us to find particular terms.

example.title: Writing Terms of Geometric Sequences Using the Explicit Formula

problem.paragraph: Given a geometric sequence with $$a_{1} = 3$$ and $$a_{4} = 24,$$ find $$a_{2}.$$

solution.paragraph: The sequence can be written in terms of the initial term and the common ratio $$r.$$
Find the common ratio using the given fourth term.

$$\begin{array}{ll} {a_{n} = a_{1}r^{n - 1}} & \\ {a_{4} = 3r^{3}} & { \text{Write the fourth term of sequence in terms of} \alpha_{1} \text{and} r} \\ {24 = 3r^{3}} & { \text{Substitute} 24 \text{for} a_{4}} \\ { 8 = r^{3}} & \text{Divide} \\ { r = 2} & \text{Solve for the common ratio} \end{array}$$
Find the second term by multiplying the first term by the common ratio.

example.paragraph: The common ratio is multiplied by the first term once to find the second term, twice to find the third term, three times to find the fourth term, and so on. The tenth term could be found by multiplying the first term by the common ratio nine times or by multiplying by the common ratio raised to the ninth power.

section.heading: Solving Application Problems with Geometric Sequences
section.paragraph: In real-world scenarios involving geometric sequences, we may need to use an initial term of $$a_{0}$$ instead of $$a_{1}.$$ In these problems, we can alter the explicit formula slightly by using the following formula:

example.title: Solving Application Problems with Geometric Sequences

problem.paragraph: In 2013, the number of students in a small school is 284. It is estimated that the student population will increase by 4% each year.

list.item: ⓐWrite a formula for the student population.
ⓑEstimate the student population in 2020.

ⓐ The situation can be modeled by a geometric sequence with an initial term of 284. The student population will be 104% of the prior year, so the common ratio is 1.04. Let $$P$$ be the student population and $$n$$ be the number of years after 2013. Using the explicit formula for a geometric sequence we get $$P_{n} = 284 \cdot 1.04^{n}$$

ⓑ We can find the number of years since 2013 by subtracting. $$2020 - 2013 = 7$$ We are looking for the population after 7 years. We can substitute 7 for $$n$$ to estimate the population in 2020. $$P_{7} = 284 \cdot 1.04^{7} \approx 374$$ The student population will be about 374 in 2020.
